name: Pituitary Hormone Deficiency of Meningeal Origin
aliases: Secondary Hypopituitarism due to Meningeal Disease

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Criteria for Secondary Hypopituitarism due to Meningeal Disease

criteria.description: Clinical evidence of deficiency in one or more anterior pituitary hormones
Radiological or histopathological evidence of meningeal pathology affecting the hypothalamic-pituitary region
Exclusion of primary pituitary or hypothalamic intrinsic disease by imaging and clinical evaluation
Laboratory confirmation of pituitary hormone deficiencies (e.g., low cortisol, low TSH, low gonadotropins)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of clinical hormone deficiency plus radiological or histopathological evidence of meningeal disease affecting the pituitary region, with exclusion of primary pituitary disorders
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis requires multidisciplinary evaluation including endocrinology, radiology, and pathology.

pathognomonic.notes: Due to LH and FSH deficiency

common.notes: May cause decreased muscle mass and fatigue
searchTerms: growth hormone deficiency causing short height
weakness and low blood pressure from adrenal failure
fatigue and dizziness due to adrenal insufficiency
symptoms of secondary adrenal gland failure

common.symptomName: Secondary hypothyroidism symptoms (cold intolerance, weight gain)
searchTerms: feeling cold and gaining weight from low thyroid function

common.notes: Due to mass effect or meningeal involvement near optic chiasm

occasional.symptomName: Hyponatremia due to secondary adrenal insufficiency
searchTerms: low blood sodium from adrenal insufficiency
cranial nerve palsies causing facial or eye problems

laboratory: Low serum cortisol with low or inappropriately normal ACTH
Low free T4 with low or normal TSH
Low LH and FSH with low sex steroids
Low IGF-1 indicating growth hormone deficiency
imaging: MRI showing meningeal thickening or enhancement around the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus
Absence of intrinsic pituitary mass lesions
Possible optic chiasm compression or displacement
other: Histopathological confirmation of meningeal disease (e.g., granulomatous, infectious, or neoplastic infiltration)
Exclusion of primary pituitary adenomas or hypophysitis

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of intrinsic pituitary lesions on imaging
Inflammation primarily localized to pituitary gland
Often autoimmune or lymphocytic in origin
Acute onset with sudden headache and visual loss
Hemorrhage or infarction within pituitary gland on imaging

redFlags: Rapid onset of adrenal crisis symptoms
Sudden visual field loss or diplopia
Signs of meningeal irritation or infection
